And, in fact, you seem to have squeezed in between two wheelbarrows, there seems to have been three or four, I don't know how many the tape reflects, I think actually six, but whatever the number is, and you just kind of scooted right in between those wheelbarrows; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I don't remember the wheelbarrows, but that's what seems to be in the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember that the wheelbarrows were in an area and this particular area where the wheelbarrows and items were kept for storage?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I don't remember that, know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that this area where the fence is is an area where that complex was keeping actual materials for use within the complex, such as the wheelbarrows?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I've already said: No, I don't remember that. The van pulled up and we saw the extraordinary sight of these men imprisoned behind the barbed wire and I walked towards them. I wasn't looking around me, and I hope the Court will understand that I was not trying to inspect what wasn't or was being kept in terms of wheelbarrows. I don't remember the wheelbarrows. I'm not at all contesting that they're there. They obviously are there. I didn't notice the wheelbarrows. I was looking at the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you reconcile for this Court and for me how you can, on page 104 of your book, state that the Trnopolje camp was surrounded by barbed wire in light of your testimony and in light of the tape that we've just seen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think the witness has dealt with that. Any further questions would be by way of comment. You can comment on it in due course and you can call evidence. But I think as far as this witness is concerned, the matter is exhausted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. May I have one moment? Your Honour, we do have one next segment on the tape that I need to cover with Mr. Vulliamy, if I may?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next tape, I believe, and this, Your Honour, is Defence Exhibit -- the next number, which I believe is 7 or 8, and that is a tape that was given to us by the Office of the Prosecutor which shows a different perspective again of the visit by Mr. Vulliamy at Trnopolje complex.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, if this isn't ready, it may be a convenient time --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour. We try to be efficient. Sorry. This tape right here, if we can stop -- I mean, you have paused. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you see, Mr. Vulliamy, those wheelbarrows again?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I can see the wheelbarrows, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So we're pretty much in the same area; correct, that we were in the prior tape, right, with the wheelbarrows being there?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I imagine so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Any reason to doubt it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I know it looks like the same crowd of people to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you see that house in the background?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with that house at all?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Not especially from this picture, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that I showed you a house on the prior tape?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Was that the very -- the opening shot?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I can remember you showing me a picture with a house on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I tried to direct your attention to the house. Is that or is that not the house that we saw that was outside the camp or outside the Trnopolje complex that we showed you on the first video?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm afraid I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I want you to -- you're an expert witness, I understand the Prosecution is calling you as such. I want to presume this --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to that. At no time was this witness represented as an expert witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: . The witness in this case, whatever may have been said in other cases, he is clearly a witness as to fact. You mean, I imagine, that since he was there, you want to ask him about the layout.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's said that he can't recognise the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I have just a follow-up question on that. But I must reply. If counsel is designating Mr. Vulliamy as a fact witness, I have to move, and I'm not sure if this is appropriate but I'm doing it to preserve the record, to strike the opinion testimony which Mr. Keegan elicited which at the commencement of proceedings this morning I specifically pointed out that Mr. Keegan's questions started with the fact, sir, do you have an opinion, and he gave an opinion on certain items of that. I will take his representation that this witness is not an expert witness, and I agree most definitely with Mr. Keegan that he is not an expert witness to show any type of pattern or any other issues relating to that. With that in mind, if I may proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Except for this, that although you're right that, of course, normally witnesses can't give their opinion if they're not experts, nonetheless, a witness is entitled to give his impression of events, and it's probably in that light that the questions were asked and should be understood. What weight we give to those impressions, of course, will be for us to determine, because essentially we've got to decide the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, if we can please go back to the tape and the footage we were discussing. Sir, these houses that we see in the background, are those houses that are within the complex of Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I don't know, actually. I would imagine they're across the road, but from this picture, I'm afraid I can't tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is it fair to say, sir, that the houses -- strike that. Is it fair to say that there were houses outside of the Trnopolje complex?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, there were houses around, yes. Some houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you talk a little bit about the houses. And, sir, if this is a house that is outside the Trnopolje complex -- are you following me? You know where I'm going almost. If this house is on the outside of the Trnopolje complex, shouldn't the real video footage be reversed and that these people should be looking at the house if they're in the camp looking at the houses as opposed to with their backs to the houses?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I suspect that's a matter of comment, and I don't know -- I shall ask the witness -- if he can answer it if he understood it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I didn't actually understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think this is by way of comment really.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fine. If we may just go back to this footage?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may proceed two more minutes on this issue? I apologise, Your Honour, and to the Prosecutor and Mr. Vulliamy.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, on -- we're on that video footage. Thank you. If we look at this post here, sir, and there seems to be wires going to the right of the post, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, I can see -- the post about a third of the way across from the left, do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Would it trouble the Court if I would ask the lights be dimmed a little? It makes the picture so much clearer. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Sorry to trouble you. Thank you. Yes. I can see a wire extending in both directions from the post, new wire and old wire.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, do you see the gentleman to the left of the post, sir, with the blue pants or shorts without a shirt?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Are his hands up onto a wire, or what are they up -- do you see them?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I can't quite see, but he seems to be holding onto a bit of the fence, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know if he's holding that portion of the fence that's barbed wire with both hands clutched up against that fence?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: The barbed wire seems to be going underneath the bit of wire that he's holding onto.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You can tell that from -- where underneath, if we use his body or torso as a point of reference?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Sorry? Where's the barbed wire going?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yeah. You said it was below him?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It's going, it sort of enters the frame of his torso around his shoulder and seems to lower a little and then exit at the other shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And is that you that we can barely see on the left-hand side of there, the blue shirt and the --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yeah, that looks like me. That is me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Videographer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is that a convenient moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Twenty minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are nearing an end, Your Honour, so I think we're excited, and I appreciate the Court's patience with us and the tapes that were presented and the patience of the Office of the Prosecutor as well as Mr. Vulliamy on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, in 1996, we covered briefly, and I think generally areas, and how it was part personal, part professional, that you came to see Dr. Kovacevic four years after the 1992, August 5th, 1992 meeting, and you came there, but I think you told us that you didn't have a cameraman with you and you didn't have any sort of tape recorder. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, this meeting that you were going to have with Dr. Kovacevic, was it for another book that you were writing?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No. It was as part of a series of articles which had been commissioned by my foreign editor at The Guardian just before Christmas the previous year, 1995, and the idea was to write a series of articles in which we would revisit people and themes important during the war. Military people, diplomatic people, and, among the people we thought it would be interesting to talk to, were those on whose authority we had gone to the camps in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we covered authority, if you recall, a little bit yesterday when I pointed out to you, with respect to Exhibits number 55 and 56, those were your aide-memoires, as you call them, that you wrote relating to Dr. Kovacevic and Dr. Stakic and how you used the word chairman for Dr. Stakic. Do you remember that discussion?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, is it fair to state that in light -- despite your testimony, and I say this most respectfully, despite your testimony during direct examination by the Office of the Prosecutor, when he was asking you questions about the meetings and conversations you had with Dr. Kovacevic, you didn't have your notebook with you; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I don't actually recall. To the best of my recollection, we got the notebooks out when the Court asked me to read them to you, but I don't think I had them or anything when we were talking about the testimony. I was working from memory at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I agree. And it has been a long week and it's been a couple days ago, it's hard to remember a couple days, much less four years later; wouldn't you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It depends on what you're remembering. No, I don't agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the notes, just -- let's assume for the moment that the notes that you have before you now, those two books that you kept and the one containing Dr. Kovacevic's interview that you had in 1996, that actually you didn't have them during your direct examination that Mr. Keegan elicited from you. Is it fair to say that the testimony there is more reliable than your notes or less reliable than your notes?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I would say the notes were more reliable and the aide-memoire which incorporates the questions and organises the notes. The testimony was given on memory of papers I hadn't seen for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So I'm asking you, prior to the testimony that Mr. Keegan elicited from you, were you given an opportunity to review those notes?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, but I didn't go over them in great detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, the third part of this is actually your aide-memoires, and I'll try to go slow so we can follow it because there are a couple of different concepts. We have your hand-written notes that you testified were taken contemporaneous during your meeting with Dr. Kovacevic, then we have your testimony elicited through Mr. Keegan, and then we have this third document, if you will -- can I call it that? -- which were your aide-memoires; right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the aide-memoires and your hand-written contemporaneous notes taken during your conversation with Dr. Kovacevic, which would you say were more reliable?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I'd say that the notes were taken from the conversation, they are not the entire conversation, and what we're calling the aide-memoire is, if you like, the following night on a friend's computer in Zagreb, I'm trying to organise the conversation with a view to writing an article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt to see if I understand this. Were the notes taken actually during the meeting as you were sitting there?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That was in February?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: February '96, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do we actually have a date for it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't have an exact date but I can easily get it for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, it's of no significance. Just help us with the time. What sort of time of day was it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: In the morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And then the aide-memoire, which is Exhibit 55, was made the next day, so --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: The following evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The following evening. And I think you said, correct me if I'm wrong, that it was for the purpose of an article?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just to follow up on the Court's question. Do you have that article that was published after this meeting with Dr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I don't, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When was the article published, if at all?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It would have been shortly after the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, going back to these three documents, your testimony, the aide-memoires, and your hand-written contemporaneous notes. Sir, which would be most reliable of the three?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: The contemporaneous notes, obviously, but they do not contain the questions that would explain what it is Dr. Kovacevic was answering in the notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, if you recall your testimony through Mr. Keegan during his questioning, at 16.07.23, you stated that you said -- and you're discussing this area and I'm going to the centre of it, that's why I give you the specific second portion, and you're talking to us, as you have during the last couple of days, you say: "Doctor, were you part of it." And then you said he said -- you're referring to Dr. Kovacevic; right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then you say, quote: "If I was to be acquitted of being a part of this collective madness, that would not be right, but I would want to ask myself what my part in it was." And then you say "end quote." Do you remember giving that testimony?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It's to the best of my recollection what I had written in the notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The word "collective madness," sir, does it or does it not appear in your book that was published in late 1993, 1994?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you this: If you look at your aide-memoires on that particular section, Exhibit 55, page 3, and I'm not sure that they're numbered, but it should be the third page of Exhibit 53 (sic), the first question that's asked: "Were you part of this collective madness or outside it?" And then there's the text that appears there -- you don't have that text. If I could have someone tender Exhibit 55 or the registrar tender Exhibit 55 to the witness. And while we're doing that, Your Honour, I'd like to ask leave that the closed session evidence and testimony that was presented in reading, and I believe he read it and we're verifying that, where he read his notes on this '96 meeting, be introduced and incorporated as part within this portion so the Court can review it at their leisure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It is part of the record, all that interview, and, in fact, all that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And if I may just inquire of the Court. Would it be fair to say that you need not my assistance to go through each and every inconsistency, if you will, or expansion or, we've called it distortion, and I recognise the word is strong, of the comparison between his notes and the aide-memoire and his testimony, or would the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You may take that point, and if you wish to deal with the witness by putting the matter generally, putting some particular points, you won't be subject to any criticism, and you can then take us through what you say are any inconsistencies in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Clearly -- I'm sorry. Clearly any major inconsistencies you should point out so the witness has a chance of dealing with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, we're now in the section -- in your notes and in your testimony -- strike that. In your testimony, I noted significantly that when Mr. Keegan asked you questions, he didn't put the question to you: "Mr. Vulliamy, did you ask Dr. Kovacevic, were you part of the collective madness or were you outside it?" Right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I know it's been a long week. In fact, you had asked Dr. Kovacevic the question, and it was you, sir, who inserted the words "collective madness," did you not?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: In the testimony or in the interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In the interview, sir.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: In the interview, yes, I remember -- I think it was my colleague actually said -- we were talking about the fight that the Serbs in the area had been engaged in, and, yes, my colleague asked him, "Was it a necessary fight or was it madness, a moment of madness?" I don't remember "collective madness," but I remember the term coming up in the conversation, I remember Dr. Kovacevic using it, and I remember us using it, to the best of my recollection and looking at this now, yes. I'm not trying to say that the word madness wasn't first used by us and not him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's fair. And not only was the word "madness" used but "collective madness", do you see that appearing on the question itself where you state on page 3 of Exhibit 55, quote: "Were you part of this, under scored, collective madness, et cetera?"

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure one of us asked that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can we tell by looking at Exhibit 55 whether these were your questions or your colleague's questions?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No, I'm afraid not. By and large, the first part of the conversation would have been mostly my colleague's, and the latter part mostly mine. But I'm not going to say whose is whose question because I can't now remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: During the conversation that you had with Dr. Kovacevic on February of 1996, did you have any drinks with him?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what type of drinks were they, if you could share it with the Court?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Plum brandy.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you yourself, sir, have a plum brandy with Dr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I had a glass of plum brandy, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did your colleague have a glass of plum brandy with Dr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How many did he have?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Quite a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your colleague?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: My colleague had a glass. I can't speak for him, actually, but not much.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, you were there. I'm asking you just about your colleague at the moment. We know what you've written and we'll get to that in a second. Your colleague, I'm interested to know how many glasses of brandy did your colleague have?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I don't know. I mean enough to be able to drive competently afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So he was the one who was driving you or not?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: We both drove.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I just want to know either way. Just help me out here.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: At some point in the journey that followed the interview we both drove.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is it your testimony, sir, that you had one glass of brandy at the outset of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: One glass of brandy and there was a refill about two-thirds of the way through of about a third of the glass.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you show us where it states in your hand-written notes that were taken contemporaneous with that that, in fact, you also engaged with having a drink with Dr. Kovacevic? Can you point that out to the Court?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I don't know if there is a reference. There's a reference to grapes and brandy, and there's a reference to him having some drinks, but, sorry, I don't remember. I don't think there is a reference of me having one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm familiar with the references that you made about Dr. Kovacevic, and him having drinks. Having the inability of deciphering your T-line, I just don't know if there is any reference there with respect to you having drinks?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, there isn't. And it wasn't drinks, I had a drink, and a small bit of a glass later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I stand corrected. A drink and then a refill of whatever two-thirds you said, or whatever?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: About a third, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you show the Court where on Exhibit 55, when you were doing the aide-memoires, where it indicates that you also engaged in a drink with Dr. Kovacevic during this interview?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Sorry? On the aide-memoire where does it say that I was having a drink?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I know you mention about Dr. Kovacevic. I just want to know how thorough and complete this is and how thorough and complete your notes are, and I just couldn't find it so if you could help us out?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Oh, the consumption of drinks is from my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So is it fair to say that it doesn't appear on your hand-written contemporaneous notes on February 1996 and it doesn't appear anywhere on Exhibit 55 which is your aide-memoires; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No, I can remember when -- I can remember -- I can remember the bottle emptying.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you do state, however, interestingly enough, and Exhibit 55 I think was attached to the indictment, if I think the Prosecutor has indicated that to us, it does reflect that Dr. Kovacevic had some drinks; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Indeed. He had a few drinks.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, before we get into how many and all that, was this interview with Dr. Kovacevic an important interview for you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It was reasonably important, yes. I would say it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In fact, sir, isn't it true that it was critical, for purposes of your professional duties, in terms of writing the article?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It was one of four or five interviews I was anxious to do with a view to fulfilling the assignment. That one part of the twelve articles, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Those four or five interviews then, and we'll expand it, those four or five interviews that you had in February of 1996, were they of critical importance to you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: They were important to me. Critical is your word, not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Nonetheless important, and that's fair.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: All interviews are important.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Of course. But you didn't have a cameraman with you and you didn't have a video cassette player with you; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I never use a cameraman or a video cassette. I'm a newspaper reporter, not a television reporter.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I understand that. I just want to know how important it was. Was it not, sir, in your opinion, important enough, this meeting with these four or five individuals, to come and meet with them, and we covered the time frame when you met with the Prosecutor but I'm asking you in this context as well: Wasn't it, sir, important enough for you for this critical interview, when you did your aide-memoires to at least have with you and consult after having a brandy and a third to be able to recollect and have that tape recorder play so we could determine what it is exactly that Dr. Kovacevic said to you and what it is you said to Dr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, this is all by way of comment. The witness has dealt with that matter. He said that he didn't have any of this and he's giving his evidence from the notes which he made and the aide-memoire.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Going back and I want to direct your attention again to page 3 of Exhibit 55 where we were talking about this collective madness. Sir, you mentioned Gutman (sic) a little bit about his Marxist principles and the Court inquired a little bit, and are you familiar at all with the Communist teachings at all about collective responsibility?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Could I just perhaps say that I think you don't mean Gutman, who is a colleague of mine who works for the News Day newspaper of New York and Mr. Deichmann who is the man that thinks that we fabricated the camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I stand corrected. With respect to Mr. Deichmann, there was a discussion about, and you were going to elicit Marxism, or whatever was in your answer will stand on the record. When we talk about collective madness here, and I think it's a relevant point, are you familiar with what collective responsibility is within the Communist principles at all?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I'm familiar with the term as used in Communist and other societies, including Western countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Share with us that which you know about that.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Collective responsibility, as I understand it, means, for instance, that in the Cabinet of my country, a Minister has -- is collectively responsible for the activities of the Cabinet. In the Communist system, as I understand it, it's a long time since I was a student, but as I understand it, in the Communist system, that idea of collective responsibility is more entrenched, the collectivity closer-bonded than in a Western political system.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, directing your attention again to 16.07.23, when you said Dr. Kovacevic stated, quote. And you're at this time as a point of reference quoting Dr. Kovacevic and stating that he purportedly said: "If I was to be acquitted of being part of this collective madness, that would not be right, but I would want to ask myself what my part in it was." And then I'd like for you to compare it to the page 3 of Exhibit 55 where he discusses with the word "if someone acquitted me." Can you read that, keeping in mind that we're looking at the screen as to what he said?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. My testimony from the other day is, as I recalled it, from memory, reading from this paper in front of me, which I do recognise, it says: "If someone acquitted me, saying that I was not a member of that collective madness, then I would have to admit that this was not true." And then he continues: "But I would want to think about how much I was part of it." And the rest you can read.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, if you could go to your contemporaneous notes taken of the February -- of the February '96 meeting with Dr. Kovacevic? Can you just let me know when you get to the point that we're discussing here?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It will take some -- if the Court could give me leave just to find it in the notes? Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just for the record, if you could read for us the portion immediately preceding that just so we make sure we're at the right page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which page are we on, for a start? Which page of the interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't know from his notes which page it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, could you help us which page that is?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. One, two, it's the fourth page at the top of which is the T-line word "Perhaps" which is a vertical, a diagonal, another vertical, and a little circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, where does it appear that we start to discuss --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It's the -- well, in fact, the word is, it's about two-thirds of the way down, and it's a long hand word "If."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you read that into the record for us again, please?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. "If someone said I was not a member of the collective madness, I would say that is not true, but then I would like to think about how much. It's a fact. I was a member of the municipal government," and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So this "if" starts by saying, "If someone said I was not a member of the collective madness," right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, look at your aide-memoires. How did you start it there?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: "If someone acquitted me ...."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You put "If someone acquitted me" on the document that was attached to the indictment, but it's not in this specific section that parallels your contemporaneous notes; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I didn't attach this to any indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I know you may think you didn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I'm going to object, Your Honour. That is extremely argumentative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I withdraw the comment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Looking at your aide-memoires, sir, and specifically in this sentence here: "If someone said," and then if you compare the original contemporaneous notes and those that were supplied to us as Exhibit 55 by the office of the Prosecution, sir, it says, and you added -- I think you added because I think -- Exhibit 55 is your document; right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. So you added the words "acquitted me"; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. I think given the nature of the question, that's the sense of what he was trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's your interpretation; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: That's my impression, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I want you to tell the Tribunal if you could point out for us where else did you place on Exhibit 55 your own interpretations, as you call them, of the conversation that you had with Dr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Sorry? Where did I put my interpretations?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's no need to object. He can't deal with that. If there is a particular point you want to put to the witness, do, but it's far too wide a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If you continue on, sir, on this section, can you point for the Court, point out to the Court, where you talk about this Communist mistake?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. Which document do you want me to read from?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'd like you to read the contemporaneous notes or as we've identified them as the contemporaneous notes?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: The bit about Tadic -- "We lived in 50 years of collective responsibility. That was the Communist mistake. If everything is okay in this hospital, then clearly I am responsible. If things do not -- if things are not good in this hospital, then I am guilty."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Continue to read that portion, if you don't mind?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: "I learned that all Germans are killers. Then I went to Germany and found it was not true. Every man has his good side and its bad side. Where he is is the important thing."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like for you, sir, to flip to the next page of your contemporaneous notes. Excuse me. If we may have just one moment? A point came up for clarification. If I may? Just direct Mr. Vulliamy -- and I apologise for this -- to go back one page because I want to cover this area with respect to this collective madness that we were just talking about where the acquittal issue came up?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So we're going back to page 3 now, just trying to help everyone along, due to my error. Now, if you recall your testimony with Mr. Keegan, nowhere in your testimony specifically the hour 16.07.28 through 16.08.38 do you discuss, when you're talking about this issue, that particular phrase, "We lived for 50 years in a society of collective responsibility, and that was the Communist mistake." It's not mentioned during your testimony. Is it, sir, because you just didn't recall it; would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I didn't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, if we can skip to page 4? If you could skip to midway portion of page 4. Do you see it with the little -- it says "I think you earlier testified ash something his sweater"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's page 5, in fact?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I think I've got different pages than you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's the fifth page.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: This is a bit -- sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's the notes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It's the notes, sorry. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, are you there where we talk about the ash fell his sweater?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I just want to try to find it on the aide-memoires where they are in this section. It says Bosnia something something. Can you read that into the record?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Bosnia was not a State.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, where is that in relation to Exhibit 55?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: The cigarette ash is mentioned on page 3 when he's talking about The Hague. That's just at the top of -- yes, the reference in the typewritten document is just -- well, is actually just a paragraph above where it appears in the notes. You can see the top of that page starts "This institution at the H," which is The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why don't we read that section, if you don't -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: That's where this -- to answer your question, that's where the cigarette ash reference comes in the aide-memoire.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I see it and we'll get to that. Why don't we read that section and from your contemporaneous notes, if you don't mind?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: "This institution at the H is a new institution. They have to show if they are serious. I think it's more of a political game than anything else. It's more a game than a serious (something). He is (something) man, Clinton and Milosevic."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. If you look at your aide-memoires, when you say he is an old man, who is he referring to? Himself? That Kovacevic is an old man?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No. Well, I've read the shorthand note and the aide-memoire, as I've said, was compiled after a conversation with my colleague, and I'm -- it would be cheating because I can see from here that he's talking about Richard Goldstone who was then the Prosecutor. There's presumably a question in there or he mentions Goldstone or Roger mentions Goldstone and I don't have it in the shorthand note.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That was my question. It's not anywhere in the shorthand note; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, what does it say immediately after that, after Milosevic is cited and Clinton.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: In which document?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: On your contemporaneous notes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Tito was a ruler, and it continues on. Then it says --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me just stop you, if I may? I don't see that contemporaneous with your note there, the aide-memoires. Do you see it coming right after Clinton and Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No, I don't. This isn't meant to be a transcript. If it's been described as one by somebody else other than me, that is incorrect. This is an organisation of the material. Here he goes, he's talking about Tito, I stop writing down what he's saying. These notes are not a transcript of the conversation, of every word that is said, and this is not an exact transcript. The notes resume at the following line, "But the establishment of Bosnia. Bosnia was established," da na na.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Continue to read that for us, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt on a point. An aide-memoire is a lawyer's term and I think described first of all by Mr. Ostojic in that way. It's the way that lawyers would look at it. How would you describe, Mr. Vulliamy, this document?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: This document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The typewritten one which we've called an aide-memoire. How would you describe it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I'd describe it as notes that I make that organise the rather haphazard -- I mean, the conversation, like any conversation, goes round and round, the themes come and go, they appear and reappear. There is discussion, there are questions that illuminate what is in the notes. Otherwise, you can have a paragraph that starts "It" something. It doesn't make any sense on its own. As soon as I could get to a computer, what I did was typed up what I thought were the pertinent sections of the conversation and tried to organise them thematically in such a way that I could use to write with. Aide-memoire, it was -- I didn't realise that it was a legal term. I'm not a lawyer, I'm a reporter. It's an attempt to organise, for my benefit, the material in a way that contains what are -- seem to be the important passages, organised thematically so I could write an article based on the conversation. If that's helpful, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I address the Court for a moment? Your Honour, I believe that the aide-memoire's comment was attributed to me in my inquiry. I believe the Office of the Prosecutor may stipulate to this. It is not my word and it was not used by me. Mr. Vulliamy, I think the record will definitively show that he described the document initially as being an aide-memoire, and I'm merely using his words and I'm stumbling through using them because I'm not familiar necessarily with that word, and respectfully, I know it's been a long week, I just wanted to point that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, I did not intend any criticism, I merely wanted to try and get perhaps a more accurate description. We are calling it an aide-memoire. It is a simple way to describe it. It describes it partly but not wholly. An aide-memoire is something which is written particularly for the purpose of recollecting a conversation. This also had another purpose, it appears, which was to organise the material. It's so that we could better follow the cross-examination. But no criticism of you at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, I just want to point this out, sir, that where you talk about the cigarette on the sweater, it's the sweater of Dr. Kovacevic you're talking about there; right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It might be a minor point, but I'd like to address it. Did you, in fact, add this section where you talk about the ash on the sweater, and I think you have three brandy. Did you add that after you left Dr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No. That would be contemporaneous. It's a way of working, you put anything that isn't in quotations, observations, descriptions, and so on, in a margin.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, when you were doing the, if I may be permitted to use the word aide-memoires, the next day in the evening, did you, as you were doing the aide-memoires, did you consult with and utilise your contemporaneous notes of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And when you were doing your aide-memoires, sir, how is it that the aide-memoire says "Fourth slivovic, cigar ash all over sweater and doesn't have a time but the contemporaneous notes has something different and does have a time. I'm perplexed by it. It's not a major point. And I apologise for inquiring on it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No, I agree with you it's not a major point.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How is it, though? Can you reconcile it for me?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Maybe there was one slivovic at the beginning that isn't counted here. I'm afraid I can't answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What I'm curious to know is if you had this document with you and you were typing up or putting in these aide-memoires, as we've called them, in here, how could it be that you've made that mistake?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, I don't think it's a mistake. He's had three before 10.30, there's a fourth here, I don't know how many he'd had at any point on this page, and, actually, I don't know at what point while writing that page I'd have written that note in the margin. I've put it at the top of what is that page of shorthand note having come to it first turning the page. But three or four during that page and maybe the one opposite, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you don't have the time there either as a point of reference to note on your aide-memoires whether it was in the morning, late morning, afternoon, evening, do you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, no. It was all in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But I note that in your contemporaneous notes on the side added from the text placed there -- I don't mean to give too much significance to the word "added" at this time -- but placed on the side there you have the time; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Placed on the side it says three brandies before 10.30. That is to say I don't know at which point during that page, those notes, I would have put that observation in the margin.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you flip to page 8 of your contemporaneous notes. Last page for the record. And if you could flip to the fifth page of the aide-memoires? Now, the last page of the aide-memoires that you're looking at which is page 6, so the entirety of page 6 and the bottom portion of page 5 of the aide-memoires, Exhibit 55, on this page 8, on the bottom portion, where does that section begin, if you could point that out on your contemporaneous notes?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Sorry. Where does the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Where does the bottom portion of page 6 -- strike that. Where does the bottom portion of page 5 of the aide-memoires and the entirety of page 6 on the aide-memoires, where does it appear since apparently it's on the last page of the aide-memoires, I'm assuming it's on the last page here, where on the last page do you see that near the bottom? Point it out.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It doesn't appear in the notes. This was a conversation between my colleague and Dr. Kovacevic as we prepared to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So is it fair to state that that entire section on the bottom portion of page 5 and the entire portion of page 6 doesn't appear anywhere on those reliable notes that you took that were contemporaneous with the conversation that you had with Dr. Kovacevic in February of 1996?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: That is correct. That section from "Do you know the prisoners -- did you know the prisoners in Omarska" is from memory the day after and in consultation with my colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Knowing that, what else can you share with us with respect to the aide-memoires that were in consultation with your colleague as you sit here? Any other glaring sections, sir? And take a moment, if you will, just to peruse the document?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, I'd need some time to look through it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may make that suggestion?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, there's one certainly, which is the bit about, at the beginning, Roger is doing most of the talking, and he's talking about why the Serbs were fighting, what they were scared of, being afraid of the Muslims, Dr. Kovacevic is talking about the Muslims who have left the municipality, where they are, why he's afraid of them, and he comes up with this, I think rather astute remark about snakes and lizards. That is in Roger's -- during a conversation at the beginning that he was having with the doctor and which I then place in the aide-memoire during the conversation that I was having with him about Jasenovac. That's one that comes to mind but that's just me looking at the top. As I say, this -- I'm calling it the aide-memoire -- these typewritten notes are a composite. That's one. And there may be others.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: There may be other what? Other notes?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No, no. Other occasions on which, in consultation with my colleague, I was able to type a document that made more sense thematically than the notes which were obviously taken in the order that the conversation was had.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If we just could note for the record, although it might be somewhat obvious, none of the questions that appear or none of the questions that you asked Dr. Kovacevic, they do not appear on your contemporaneous notes; right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No, they don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the introductory passages that we read yesterday from Exhibits 55 and 56, they likewise don't appear on the contemporaneous notes, do they?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Sorry, the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Introductory language that you have on Exhibit 55.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Forgive me, Your Honour. Which is Exhibit 55?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's to your right, if I may direct the witness.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Oh, this?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: The ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Introductory paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No, this is a recollection and this is setting it in context.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You testified and we were unclear when I reviewed the transcript from yesterday, and forgive me for going back to this issue, the disk that you had, that you used to type up what was ultimately provided to the office of the Prosecution, and then you used the word in that discussion, the original. Were you talking about the original or original summary of your conversation with Dr. Kovacevic that would have been on that disk?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Original summary? I'm talking about --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Original aide-memoire, sorry.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I'm talking about this document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is this the only -- is this the document -- if I were to one day obtain that disk, and I know you promised -- or you mentioned that you are going to endeavour to find it for us, if you find that disk, is it your testimony that that disk will be exactly like this document appears?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: When the disk left me, it would have had this and the conversation with Dr. Stakic and two other conversations on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the two other conversations were with Major Milutinovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the fourth one was with whom?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Nikola Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you had those two conversations with those two individuals before you actually met with Dr. Kovacevic; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No. As I recall, that with Major Milutinovic was the day before, and that with Professor Koljevic was the morning after -- sorry that with Professor Koljevic was two days after on a different visit to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Two days after your conversation with Dr. Kovacevic; right?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you look through your contemporaneous notes for me, the couple of pages before Dr. Kovacevic's contemporaneous notes?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Two pages before Dr. Kovacevic's --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: A couple.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're now going into material that is beyond the scope of direct, and this is of course was material that was -- issues that were raised in closed. I'm just concerned where we're going here with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As a point of reference, I want to verify, Your Honour, exactly whether or not there were notes taken -- and I'm tipping my hand, which is fair, and that's fine -- with respect to Professor Koljevic's meeting, whether he has notes of that meeting before the notes that he took now of Dr. Kovacevic or after or the notes of -- because we had seen one thing at a private session that we had with the office, so that's why I'm inquiring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can ask if the notes were taken.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, and I'm happy to answer. The two pages before the interview with Dr. Kovacevic are headed "Milutinovic," and they're with Major Milutinovic. The pages that follow Dr. Kovacevic are the interview with Mr. Stakic, then again -- oh, then early next morning, there's an interview with another gentleman, and then sometime later, Professor Nikola Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may direct the witness to go to the materials immediately prior to where he mentioned the two pages of his conversation with Major Milutinovic, and if he could identify -- and I ask him to keep in mind the Court's ruling on the limitations of this, so I don't want him to blurt anything out that's inappropriate or something, but I want to know if there's any mention, prior to Major Milutinovic, of Professor Koljevic's.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Any mention of Mr. -- let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is it that you want so we can follow?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Any summary of notes relating to Dr. Koljevic that may appear prior to Major Milutinovic's meeting. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: If it helps the Court, what I could do is work backwards from the beginning of the Kovacevic interview, and using my discretion, tell you what's on which page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you could help me. What's the point of all this?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I think it really, to be honest -- to be candid with the Court, as I think we all have been here, when we were at the conference, we believe several of those pages were noted. His testimony now, in our opinion, Your Honour, was somewhat inconsistent. I could move along if the Court wishes me to move along --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think we are going to be helped by this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, if I were to tell you that we attempted to examine your specific contemporaneous notes with your aide-memoires, which is Exhibit 55, and if I tell you that we found approximately -- or, actually, over 50 inconsistencies, some minor -- and we noted the very big paragraph and we noted the word "acquittal," would you find that to be surprising?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't. There are a number of considerations. One is the need to organise things thematically. The other consideration is this, that Dr. Kovacevic is an articulate man, and quotations of articulate people should not always be left with the grammar of the translator, so that if -- you know, if the translator says, as it does in the shorthand notes, "Every man has its good side and its bad side," you turn that into "his good side and his bad side." So this is not intended to be an exact transcript of the shorthand.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: A couple more questions, if I may? You discussed a little bit with Mr. Keegan this snake-lizard analogy, if you will; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, I thought it was astute --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I could introduce for just one moment, and if you could find it for us in your contemporaneous notes, and I'll direct the Court and your attention that that section seems to appear on page 3, bottom portion. Can you tell us, Mr. Vulliamy, where the lizard-snake discussion appears on the contemporaneous notes?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. I think I already have, actually. It's in the first bit of the conversation which is mostly between my colleague and Dr. Kovacevic, of which I took some notes but by no means complete, and they're talking about the -- why the Serbs went to war, they are talking about the Serbian fear, the Second World War, and Mr. Kovacevic's own background, and I thought the point he made about snakes and lizards was particularly astute. The conversation that I am having with him later on about his background comes in later, as you can see, and I put it down there in my reorganisation of the material because I didn't want to lose it. I thought it was a rather astute point.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And, sir, I just wanted an answer to my question. I'll try to rephrase it a little better. On page 3 of Exhibit 55, this issue with the cigarette ash over the sweater, we know that that appears on page 5 of your contemporaneous notes, right? "Cigarette ash on sweater"?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: "Three brandies," you note the time, and then here you have four Slivovic; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, the three of your were -- you, your colleague, and Dr. Kovacevic -- were there; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: And the translator.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who is that translator?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It's a man called -- actually, I'd rather not use his name, if that's okay? He came from Bijeljina and was an experienced man.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, if I may just inquire, on the translator, a question or two. Was that the same translator that accompanied you in 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In fact, just so my question doesn't later -- or a claim doesn't be made on my question that it wasn't extensive. You had two translators in 1992. Was the translator that you had in February of 1996 any of the two that you had in '92?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No, neither of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, we're looking on page 5 of your contemporaneous notes, and respectfully, on page 3 of Exhibit 55, where we're talking about "fourth Slivovic, cig. ash all over sweater." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Show me here where, immediately thereafter or so you discuss -- strike that. Why don't you be kind enough, because when I asked you the question what page it was, you gave us your answer, but I didn't catch the page number. Just tell me what page number on your contemporaneous notes does the snake-lizard analogy appear?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: At the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I know the beginning.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Page 1. Where on page 1?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: In the first -- the second paragraph, the first big paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's underscored, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It's underlined, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now as a word --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Some of it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you read the words that appear right immediately before "snake" that I see in the middle right-hand portion of page 1 of your contemporaneous notes?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: "When you are unlikely or unlucky."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Then you may proceed to read that, please?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: "When a snake bites you, you are afraid of little lizards, but a lizard is" -- sorry. "A lizard is still a lizard but a snake is a snake. I am worried about the future."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You testified through questioning by Mr. Keegan, would it be fair to say, a little broader on that discussion, and you put quotes around certain things on the snake. Would it be fair to say, sir, that that was your interpretation during that testimony of Mr. Keegan (sic) wherein you described what it was that Dr. Kovacevic purportedly meant when he was discussing with you the lizard-snake?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, he was discussing it with my colleague, actually, who was opening the conversation, and they were talking about the fact that the Serbs had been persecuted by the Croats and that he feared the Muslims, and the gist was -- and he was talking about the Serbian experience around the area and in the camps -- I wasn't paying much heed to that -- well, I was listening -- and they were talking about the fact that -- I mean the gist was, my interpretation was, and I think it's an accurate one, that the Serbs had been bitten by, if you'll pardon me for putting it this way, "the Croatian snake," but that once you're bitten by a snake, you're afraid of a lizard. And Roger asked him, "So are the Muslims the lizards? Are you scared of the Muslim lizards?" And he said "Yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Where does it say that in your contemporaneous notes or in your notes that you prepared the night after this meeting where he states, "I am scared of the Muslims"?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: That was one of Roger's questions, that he's scared of the Muslims. He's talking about that and, I, actually, before you asked me about this section, volunteered it, as the example that came first to mind of the -- how this document was reordered after a conversation with Roger who was having that -- during whose exchange with Dr. Kovacevic this, I think, rather illuminating line about snakes and lizards came up.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I couldn't disagree with you more. I could not disagree with you more, and here's why: We went through your closed session testimony on the time, and if I told you this, Mr. Vulliamy, that the only section that seems to be taken out of context is specifically this section, and that's the only section -- everything else follows with respect to the time frames, and I invite, obviously the Tribunal, as well as the Office of the Prosecution, to go through that closed session carefully and to examine that. What else, as you sit here, do you know was taken in different parts other than this section on the snakes?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I don't know. I haven't been through it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, was this your question on the snakes or was it the question of your colleague?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He said it was the colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's my point. I just wanted to recollect on that, didn't want to try to distort it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you decipher for us, looking on Exhibit 55, which questions you asked and which questions your colleagues asked -- or your colleague asked?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No. I'd have recalled it at the time, now I'm afraid I don't. By and large, towards the beginning of the conversation, the majority of the questions are those of my colleague; towards the end, the majority are mine. And as I've already testified, this very last section is a conversation between him and Dr. Kovacevic after we had stood up and made to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I want to point out one last thing, if I may? On page 4 of the aide-memoires, the bottom portion where there's a discussion about hurricane, do you see that, five or six lines from the bottom?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I'm on the right page. Could you give me the page again, sir, sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: On the aide-memoires, Exhibit 55, it would be page 4. Are you there with me?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The word "hurricane" is what we're focusing on here. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you see that? I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you just find this section first on your contemporaneous notes?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. Got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you direct us to the page of the contemporaneous notes, please?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It's one, two, three, four, five, six, seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So it would be page 7; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yeah, the penultimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: The penultimate page.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Where on the page?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: The penultimate page.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you direct us to that section where you mention the word "hurricane blowing to and fro"?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, it's just after he's giving the numbers of people "killed" in Omarska as opposed to "died" in Omarska, and you can see a sign, which is like a diagonal, then straight, and then a little circle meaning "its" and the words "wind tunnel," indeed in longhand.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'm looking for the word "hurricane" at the moment, but we'll get to wind tunnel in a second. So where is the "hurricane"? Does it appear there?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: "Hurricane" isn't there, actually. I shall read what I've written in shorthand --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's all I want to know, whether it appeared there or not.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Kovacevic used two different words, and the second with considerable emphasis, and I spoke to the translator afterwards and thought that "hurricane" would do credit both to the point he was making and to his own command of language. The repetition of "wind" -- he didn't repeat the same word, and I consulted with the translator about that. We were talking in the car that little bit about the wind blowing to and fro, and the translator filled us in.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So it was the translator who said, "Really, this 'wind tunnel' is 'a hurricane'"?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, he did. I mean -- please understand, this conversation was fairly surprising, and we talked about it on the way from Prijedor, and the -- that line stuck in my mind particularly, and the translator said he had used a different word.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I have a moment, Your Honour? Thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, in looking at your testimony and consulting here, what else did the translator or interpreter assist you with on the car ride home?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I think that was the only main point.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, what other minor points, if you could share with us?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I don't remember, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But you do remember there were some minor points; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, I don't, actually, but I remember us talking about --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who else did you consult with after the meeting with Dr. Kovacevic? You mentioned the interpreter, you mentioned your colleague. Anyone else before you wrote the aide-memoires?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No. I got back to Zagreb and told a friend about what a surprise it was, and, of course, I consulted with my office as soon as I got to a telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to Dr. Kovacevic's sobriety, and we're talking about this page 8, how would you have described it -- page 7 where we're at, how would you have described it at this point?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I'll be guided by the Court on that answer. I mean, the bottle of brandy was empty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What impression did he make on you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: He was not sober.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And at this point, sir, in the meeting, page 7, where you're telling us that he was not sober, isn't that the first time you actually put in quotes -- and you were kind enough to share it with us in your prior answer -- where you said "killed" not "died"; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. I don't see it at the moment, but I know exactly where you mean, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm inviting you to look.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I've got it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So was it at that point that your testimony is that he was not sober?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: He's not sober by this point, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you cut it off for me anywhere and show me where you think, based on these eight pages, that you believe he was not sober?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No, I can't draw a line between sobriety and non-sobriety, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me approximately where it appears, if at all?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No, I can't really. I can only say courteously that he was becoming progressively less sober.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you record that anywhere, sir, on your contemporaneous notes, that your impression of Dr. Kovacevic at that point was that he was not sober?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No, I don't on the contemporaneous notes, apart from this reference to the third glass, to the best of my knowledge, no. I'm relying, I think justifiably, on my memory there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In your aide-memoires, do you record anywhere that you felt that Dr. Kovacevic was not sober?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: On the aide-memoire?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm putting in various glasses of brandy. I don't, at any point, I don't think say "He is drunk," but my recollection and my testimony is that he was by the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you talk about this empty bottle at the end of the meeting. Was the bottle full when you started the meeting?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I don't recall, but if it wasn't full, it was nearly full.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With respect to your aide-memoires -- strike that. With respect to the article that you wrote subsequent to your conversation with Dr. Kovacevic, do you state in that article that Dr. Kovacevic was not sober during the meeting?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I don't recall, actually, but I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When was the article written, in terms of time frame, from your contemporaneous notes, from your aide-memoires and again, of course, the article?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, about two or three days later. I sat down and wrote the article containing the interviews with Drs. Kovacevic, Stakic, and Professor Koljevic, perhaps two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did Dr. Kovacevic have an attorney with him present during the conversation that you had with him in February 1996?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you also told us that Dr. Stakic was interviewed by you in February 1996. He was interviewed before or after Dr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: After.
