utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, did Dr. Stakic have with him anyone during your conversations in February 1996?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And, sir, we'll look at Exhibit 56, if you will, which I believe is the aide-memoires of Dr. Stakic. Thank you. Do you have that before you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, in there, does it mention that Dr. Stakic at all had anyone present during the meeting with him?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Could I just have a look, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. There's a reference here to that man. His name is Kondic. He was variously introduced during the conversation with a number of titles.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Was one of his titles that he was an attorney?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, as I recall, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you find that odd that there was an attorney there with Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, no, because by then the conversation was getting pretty strange, and he was initially introduced as the assistant in the health centre. Perhaps he was both. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So to this day, you don't know what he was, whether he was an attorney, an assistant to the health centre, or anything else; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, just if I may be given a bit of latitude to return to the bottle of brandy that was discussed with Dr. Kovacevic, and I have four, possibly less questions on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, how big was the bottle?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: The size of a wine bottle.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you said it was near the top. Do you know how many shot glasses, if you will, are contained within that bottle?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I don't, actually. But I should say ten or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, how big the glass -- do you recall how large the glasses were that you and Dr. Kovacevic drank from?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I don't very well, but if I could, again a guesstimate, and that's all I'm prepared to give the Court, that sort of height, a short drink glass. A cocktail glass, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's fair to state that Dr. Kovacevic had the same-sized cocktail as you did; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Same sized glass.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Same sized glass. Thank you. Yes?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In your aide-memoires with respect to Dr. Kovacevic, how many do you say, how many shots did he have or how many drinks?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I've given it back, actually, but I think he had seven or eight.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you point out to me -- and forgive me for having the registrar share with him that document again. Your memory is quite good, but I'll direct your attention to page 5 of your aide-memoires.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You want to tell us it's seven or eight. On page 5, how many does it say in the middle of the page?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Six.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Show the Court where you think your aide-memoires say that it was seven or eight?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I want to ask a question here relating to the lizard-snake, if you will. Two questions. Have you ever heard the phrase -- have you ever heard the phrase "Once bitten, twice shy"?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, I've heard that, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you explain what that means?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I think it means that -- well, I'm not sure, actually. I think it means once you get stung, you're going to be reticent twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is that what Dr. Kovacevic was talking about when he discussed the lizard-snake, in your words?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No. As I understand it, we were talking about the fact that once you get bitten by a snake, you're afraid of little lizards, and the context of the conversation, as I've said, was the experience of the Serbs and their persecution at the hands of the Croats and that that was making them scared of lizards, and we talked about Muslim lizards.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I know that's what you want to say. But I want you to go back to page 1 of Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object again. This is argumentative again. He's asking questions, he's getting answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You can ask the question, but we have been through this, you know? If there's any new point you can make --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I do. One last point.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If we can go to page 1 of that eight-page contemporaneous note, please?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you attribute that comment at all with quotation marks, because I note in the closed session, if I may be permitted, that -- well, the closed session will speak for itself. Let me ask you now: Do you attribute any quotation marks around that comment?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. It starts off with a quotation before the word "When," I close the quote after "lizards," but then cross out the closing of the quote because he still appears to be quoting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When does he end the quote?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It doesn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Does there seem to be a line going after the word "snake" on the right-hand portion, a faint line on my copy; it may just be a photocopy error?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: You mean this little line going down the side of the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Where is that directing us to?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may ask you, sir, for purposes -- and we discussed earlier in your testimony distortion and things that are distorted or things that are misrepresented, et cetera. Would it be fair to say, sir, that when you added the word before -- or "if I am acquitted," that that would be a misrepresentation, a distortion, or how would you describe it for us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I think we've been through all that, and that's a matter of comment. Yes. Anything new?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever at any time, sir, study Shakespeare?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No, I never studied Shakespeare since school, but I've read Shakespeare ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you recall a phrase that people attribute to lawyers within writing of Shakespeare where he says: "The first thing we should do is kill all the lawyers?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, I think we're going a very long way from the subject of this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm going to connect it up, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That sounds like a comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, I am going to connect it up, Your Honour. I just want to know him if he's familiar with it and ask for his understanding in this context.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I don't know that line from Shakespeare. I don't recognise it from any Shakespeare play that I've read.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm just telling you and I'm representing that that comment, having been used, and if you look at that comment right there, "The first thing we should do is kill all the lawyers," seems to suggest one thing, but, in fact, when I was a young lawyer and someone made that comment and we researched it and we found that within -- I think it was Hamlet, but it may have been McBeth - forgive me for not being accurate - the phrase attributed to Shakespeare was that "If we want anarchy, the first thing we do is kill all the lawyers." Can you tell how different those two things can be and how they can be taken out of context?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not going to allow this. I think it's Richard the II, but it's totally irrelevant. Let's go on. Have you got anything else for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned -- Your Honour, at this time, I need to have a moment to find an exhibit regarding the International Red Cross, and it's not at my fingertips and I may have left it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's see if we can find it. Which one is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's an exhibit that was attached, and I'm going to mispronounce the name, Mazowiecki was the --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Mazowiecki. Tadeusz Mazowiecki.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have it. It's Exhibit 52. Thank you. But before we begin with Exhibit 52, I would ask the Court's permission, with this group of documents, to know whether we have been provided the date of the first exhibit that I believe Judge Cassese respectfully asked counsel to provide us with. I just need to know the date and I will need to inquire possibly depending on the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I must confess, Your Honour, that over the course of the days, it slipped my mind to pull that. I remember it came up in Tadic and it was found -- I think it may even be in the record of the Tadic case, but I did neglect to pull it out. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It can be provided in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, returning to Exhibit 52, that was an article written on or about October 23rd, 1992; correct? And I'll wait for you to get the document. Are you with me, Mr. Vulliamy?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I'm getting there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm just merely waiting for Mr. Vulliamy.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, the question was: This article appeared on or about October 23rd, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: As I've testified, I recall the report. I recall several reports by Mr. Mazowiecki. This is an Agence France Presse report of the report, so I don't recall this actual report, but I do know what they're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you have an opinion, sir, of Mr. Mazowiecki at all that you've formulated over the years?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: What? Do I think he's a good man?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you think he's a good man? Do you think, when he reports, he reports accurately?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not sure this is a matter for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I want to know if he's formulated that opinion. I just don't know if he has or hasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can ask the witness about the report, by all means, but not about the reporter.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: From the bottom -- thank you -- the third paragraph from the bottom one, it says: "Mazowiecki said that in Trnopolje ..." Are you with me?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Does he say in that paragraph that the Bosnian Muslim homes were destroyed or burned, or does he use the word "all"?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: In this AFP report of what he said, it says "all." It's not in quotes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If you look at the last paragraph, do you know who Paul Henri Morad is?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I know who he is, but I've never met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who he is?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: He's an official of the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And, sir, do you see there, on the last sentence of paragraph 3, how the ICRC, in October 23rd, 1998 (sic), describes this Trnopolje and the people that were in it; do you see the last two words? How does he describe them?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Sorry. Which --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The very last two words, sir, on that article, Exhibit 52.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: "Detention camps."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I may have misspoken and said '98. I think the record's rather clear that Exhibit 52 is October 23rd, 1992. Your Honour, at this point, I believe that it would be convenient to take a short recess so that I can consult to ensure that all the areas -- and consult with Dr. Kovacevic, if permitted -- to ensure that all the areas are covered -- as well as with my colleagues here -- are covered with respect to Mr. Vulliamy. Maybe ten or fifteen, Your Honour, if I may? Because they're going to have to take him and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can have ten minutes, but this examination of the witness must finish today and, of course, there's re-examination, and the Trial Chamber has some questions itself. So would you bear that in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will, and I am labouring forward, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I just want to -- so that you know where I'm going. I'm almost done. Maybe two or three questions on follow-up. I have to insist -- I have to request that I be permitted just to revisit for those two or three questions the proverb that was put in quotes of the lizard and the snake, and we hope to put it in context, but we just want to be clear on that. May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If possible, you can confine your questions to ten minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will. No longer than that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, was this a proverb, that you put in quotes, about the snakes and the lizards?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I don't know, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did the interpreter that was with you, did she tell you at any time that it was a proverb?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: He, actually. I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's my understanding that the proverb was, and I'm going to read it in the record in the language that was given by Dr. Kovacevic, if I may? (Interpretation follows) "Whoever was bitten by a snake ends up being afraid of lizards too."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could that be repeated, please, for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Are you asking me, Your Honour? (Interpretation follows) "Whoever was bitten by a snake ends up being afraid of lizards."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, would you agree with me, sir, someone who has an understanding of a couple different languages or knows a couple different languages, that proverbs interpreted from one language to possibly English -- let's take Italian, I believe that you said you're familiar with and have an understanding of. If take an Italian proverb and interpret it into English, it may lose some, all of its meaning; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: That could happen, but this remark went on a bit longer than the translation I got here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the remark that went on a little longer we covered in your contemporaneous notes where, in fact, it ends right after that, does it not?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember, actually. On the translation, I just heard the words "ends up being afraid of lizards," or something. I didn't actually get the first half. But it's something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Could it be that the proverb may mean: Once bitten, second time shy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've asked that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have? Your Honour, at this time, with Mr. Vulliamy, and in light of our discussions with his contemporaneous notes, and we haven't deciphered them completely, we are working very methodically to obtain that, but at this time we do not believe we have any further questions of Mr. Vulliamy, and we will introduce as an exhibit his book and other items that we shared with the court today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Very brief, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: First I would like to play the video marked Prosecution Exhibit 46, Your Honour. I did manage to get -- I hopefully got it sufficiently cued during this short recess to clear up the issue of the fences and where this compound is. If you could run the tape, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If you could pause the tape, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vulliamy, you spoke first, in relation to the questions on cross-examination, about your approach to the top of the camp, the view that you saw, and what prompted you to head to that area. In relation to the footage you just saw, and I'm going to ask them to continue, and it's a very brief section here, could you indicate to the Court whether that is a representation of the view that first greeted you? Could you roll the tape at normal speed, please?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It's a rather close shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Stop the film, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Would you like me to replay it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It's all right. There's some people with a camera, but I'm not sure who that is, walking towards it. This would seem to be a part of the compound. Yes. If you're asking what made us stop, it was, as I've said before, it was the sight of a crowd of men, some of them in skeletal condition, behind a barbed wire fence, which is enough to make anyone stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Could you run the tape all the way back to the beginning there and start it again?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And, please, if you'd note closely, the initial frames here, Mr. Vulliamy?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Stop the film, please.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: That's the -- yeah, that's the area that we were approaching, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If you could fast-forward to one minute two seconds, please. This goes to the issue of the question regarding the fences, Mr. Vulliamy. If you could back it up just a few frames, perhaps to, say, one minute? Thank you. Play from there, normal speed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Stop the film there, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, can you describe what you see in that frame, please?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I can see what appears to be the or a corner of the compound at which the barbed wire fence, which caught our attention, obviously, you can see old barbed wire reinforced by new, cleaner barbed wire, and that fence behind which this man is standing then joins another fence at the corner, which appears to be what I call chain-link fencing of the kind used in gaols in the United States and, I believe, in Ulster.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Run the tape at normal speed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If you could now fast-forward the tape, please, to 1.24? We may actually be there. If you could pause the tape there?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, you were asked earlier questions about the length of the compound in which this was in. Does that assist you at all?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, there we can see from the fence through which we were talking to the prisoners to the back of that compound within Trnopolje, the wall. I gave the Court my guesstimate of two and a half football fields, and it seems to be roughly corroborated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If you could fast-forward the tape to 5 minutes, please, on the tape? And play at normal speed, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, does this perspective -- hold it right there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Does this perspective help you complete the description of your compound?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, it assists me, yes. This is another corner. We've seen this post from another view during cross-examination, I think. This would be where another bit of the barbed wire fence meets another run of chain-link fencing in another part of the compound in which the prisoners are held.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If you could play the tape at normal speed, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Does that reflect the back side, if you will, of that compound?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. It's the side of the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If you could go back now to just about the five-minute mark, five minutes, five seconds? That's it. Just back a bit, please? Okay. Play at normal speed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And if you could pause there? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, does that image again give you a better perspective of the house which the Defence asked you about and where it would be located in relation to the compound?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, I think it would be outside the compound, and I expect it's on the other side of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you. We're finished with the tape, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, did the fact that you interviewed the accused in February of 1996, did that fact have any relation to the fact that you had been contacted by the Office of the Prosecutor with respect to the case of Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No, it was an assignment from my newspaper. I've said this. I was assigned to retrace the war and to interview some of the major players in it. Others on the list included people like General Morillon. There were a large number of people. It ended up as a series of twelve articles of which this interview was part of one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Before the interview actually occurred on that morning in February of 1996, did you have a guarantee that you were going to have an interview with Dr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If he had said no to the interview, would that have terminated your project, or would you have gone on to interview other people for the series?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I'd have gone on to seek out Dr. Stakic and Professor Koljevic. We had already that morning endeavoured to -- sorry, the previous day, forgive me -- endeavoured to make contact with Mr. Drljaca but without success.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Does the witness still have Exhibit 55, which is the typed notes of the interview with Dr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I would refer you to the heading section on the first page. Questions were raised about the issue of the brandy, the time of day that the interview took place, and the fact that you had a specific time in your notes which wasn't referenced directly in the notes. Can you begin with the paragraph saying "He is now director ..."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: "He is now director of the city hospital. He is an anaesthetist by training. Atmosphere is genial. Gets a bottle out of the cupboard. 10.00 a.m."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: We have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I have, first of all, a request. I wonder whether I could ask either the witness or the parties to provide us with a copy, a photocopy, of the articles you eventually published as a result of your interviews? Is it possible? It may not be considered as evidence, but I think they might assist the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. I think the Office of the Prosecutor would undertake to provide -- obtain copies and provide that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Which will also be passed on, of course, to the Defence. Thank you. I have two questions. One question is about your trip to Belgrade. You said that after Dr. Karadzic went to London, you decided to go and visit the Omarska camp. Why did you go to Belgrade first before going to Pale?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was the stipulation of those in whose hands we are, namely Dr. Karadzic, that we would have to make our way to Belgrade and to be appropriately met and accredited with the authorities -- the press agency in Belgrade and that that is where they wanted to meet us. Our, if I may say, hostess was a woman called Mandic, and it was there that we first met Professor Koljevic and were taken from there to Pale later on, as I explained. Belgrade was their choice. Also, that was the nearest plane you could get to Belgrade, was to Hungary and that's -- so we went from there. Belgrade was where they told us to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. So you got there your accreditation through the SRNA, the Yugoslav Serbian News Agency, but the accreditation was valid in Bosnia-Herzegovina, so you got it in Belgrade for Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I can only presume so, yes. Our first instructions from the authorities in Belgrade were that to pursue this trip, to pursue this acceptance of the invitation to inspect the camps, we would first have to accredit ourselves with the SRNA. That was our very first move, our very first appointment the morning after we arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. And by and large did you -- at some point you said that the helicopter you used to go from Belgrade to Pale was provided by the JNA. Is that correct or ...

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, that's certainly my recollection. The helicopter left from a premises that was very obviously a depot of some kind of the JNA. It may have been the Yugoslav air force, but I don't think it was. I think it was the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Generally speaking, while you were there in that period, in August '92, did you have the opportunity to observe the relations between Bosnian Serb authorities and the Serbian authorities, the Belgrade authorities? Were there any occasions where you saw members of the JNA talking or discussing matters with members of the army of what later became Republika Srpska, namely the Bosnian Serbian army?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: My direct experience of military cooperation during that visit was this fact of the helicopter ride which was, if you like, seamless between the JNA base, or whatever it was from whence we left, to the Pale area where we landed. Militarily, my own personal experience is limited to the, if you like, the non-frontier at Loznica, and I described the garrison atmosphere on the Serbian side with the soldiers criss-crossing the border, but I have to say that most of my experience during that trip of entwinement between the two was more the politicians, that is to say, Professor Koljevic in Belgrade and so on. So far as I know, the soldiers who escorted us from Pale to Banja Luka were members of the Bosnian Serb army. I don't know whether those who came with us on the helicopter, of whom there were a number, were members of the JNA or the Bosnian Serb army. They seemed indistinguishable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: And when you, after August '92, went back to Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you have an opportunity again to observe the relations, if any, between the JNA and the Bosnian Serb army, or did you --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Forgive me, Your Honour. Could I just ask you the date again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: '92. Let us stick to '92. I don't know whether you had an opportunity when you went back in '92, after August '92, to Bosnia-Herzegovina, whether you were also in that area, in the area under the control of the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No, I wasn't during 1992, which was the scope of our discussion, I think. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. If I can move to a different matter? While you were commenting on your contemporaneous notes, you, at one point -- you spoke about the so-called "road bit," the bit regarding -- you gave a sort of heading, "The road bit."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You said that you saw Muslim houses where the Muslim inhabitants had put up a white flag, and I think you asked somebody a question "Why?" And the answer was, "They are waiting to leave." Now, can you elaborate on this point? Were there particular families, groups of Muslims, who had decided to put up a white flag and why, for what purposes? Apparently there were various groups of Muslims. Some of them had decided to put up this white flag and then therefore to leave, probably undisturbed, first question; and secondly, do you know whether they were allowed to leave the territory by themselves in convoys or escorted or just to go abroad?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: The question of the white flags, and there were sheets and pillowcases or whatever, was raised with Major Milutinovic twice: once on the way to Prijedor, and that was when he said they had accepted the new order, to the best of my recollection. On the back roads between Prijedor and Omarska, there were also these flags and pillowcases being hung, and I remember asking again, and this time the explanation had changed slightly, and it was that they were waiting to leave. In my own experience, the only way to leave was either in a convoy, either directly or via Trnopolje, over the mountain roads that I described in my evidence, or along a similar route about which I have no direct, as it were, inside experience, through Karlovac into Croatia up until the date that the border was sealed, as I explained. I imagine there might have been other people who left in different circumstances. There was the girl in Bihac who seemed to have been part of a smaller column being, according to her, violently pushed over the river Una into Bihac, I've testified about her, and so I can't really answer your question, but my impression is that the overwhelming majority of those who left, left in the organised convoys either directly or through Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: My point was, did you ask why some Muslims were taken to centres, detention centres, transit centres -- let us leave aside the proper label -- in three centres or areas or camps which have been mentioned, and others were allowed to stay in their houses, put up a white flag, and then were allowed to leave the territory probably in convoys? Were there particular criteria? On basically what particular criteria?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: If there were, I'm afraid I was unable to discern them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Again, a small point. At one point, you mentioned official decrees, the passing by the Bosnian Serbian authorities, official decrees deciding whether or not Muslims were allowed to stay in villages near Prijedor. Am I correct in saying that you, at one point, mentioned these decrees about categories of Muslims which were allowed and some other categories which were not allowed to stay there but were asked to leave or forced to leave?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I think so, yes. Again, I don't know what qualified you to be allowed to stay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But did you see any of those decrees?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: There was a decree which a colleague of mine on The Guardian got in a village called Selinac about which he wrote and showed me the document, and that was the document that specifies that Muslims are not allowed to meet in groups of three -- groups of more than three, et cetera, which I alluded to earlier. But I don't know, I really can't answer you, as to what qualified a Muslim to stay or to leave. All I do know is that in -- if I may just mention another date? In 1995, at the crossing point near Travnik through which I had passed three years earlier, there were still trickles coming through. I would be going outside my ambit to talk about what they were saying, but they had stayed on in circumstances which I think we've seen described in some of the Red Cross exhibits, difficult ones, but I don't know what qualified them to say. I'm afraid I can't help you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I see from your answer that -- yes, you are right. Actually, my notes were wrong. What you said about these official decrees were, you said that those decrees specified what Muslims were allowed to do and what they were not allowed to do in those villages near Prijedor, so categories of behaviour or conduct -- so this is one of those decrees?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. This is just one village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I wonder whether we could be provided by the parties or by the witness copies of those decrees because they might be of some assistance to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: We have a witness, Your Honour, who will be testifying during the next session, who will be able to introduce the specific document that Mr. Vulliamy is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I am through with my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just address the Court to follow up just a couple of minor clarifications after Judge Cassese addressed the witness. It's basically SRNA, and I think there was a misquotation what does it mean, and it seems by implication it could suggest that it was a Yugoslav agency, and if either Judge would like to clarify what the words mean and what that acronym is supposed to mean, who did he see in Belgrade, and why Dr. Karadzic went via Belgrade and why did he invite them to go via Belgrade, were there any other routes that were at that time open, because it seems that kind of does not elucidate all the points that Judge Cassese wanted to examine on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I didn't understand you, sorry. Were you asking me to ask questions to the witness? I agree -- I agree with you that it's a matter if the witness could clarify this point. First of all, the acronym. The acronym, this SRNA. The witness said, when he was examined in chief, that this meant Yugoslav Serbian News Agency. Do you know what --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY
utterances.text: So far as I know, Your Honour, it's CRNA, and I don't know what it stands for.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: It's S-R-N-A, SRNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be that we'll get some evidence about what that means in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Could I just give him a hypothetical? If I were to tell you that that stands for Serbian Republic News Agency, would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to this. This is improper questioning of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll find out in due course. We'll find out in due course. If that's right ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Probably the witness could be so kind as to add a few comments about the persons he met while in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The first person who met us at the hotel which, as I recall, was chosen by us, the Hyatt Hotel, was called Klara Mandic. She said she represented something called the Serbian Jewish Friendship Society. I don't know why that in particular. She then made the introductions to Professor Koljevic that evening, I think, and some other officials and a television producer, as I recall. It was at her request that we went to register at the SRNA -- I'm not in a position to either agree or disagree with counsel on what that stands for. To this day, I don't know. But whatever it is, they had an office in Belgrade, and we went down there and filled in various forms, I think paid a very small fee for registration of some kind, tiny amount, and apart from that, we -- well, we had this one meeting at the Hyatt. Then we were waiting around, actually, to go, making these various trips to -- day trips to Loznica, another place nearby called Subotica as part of our inspections of the names on the list the Bosnian government had put out, and I've already talked about those places. But apart from that, I'd say that the people we -- yes, the people we met in Belgrade, those were the main ones. I don't recall the names of any others. And then the morning came when Mrs. Mandic came to instruct us to go to the helicopter pad, which I don't think belonged to the Serbian Jewish Friendship Society, and that was our experience of Belgrade. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vulliamy. Thank you for coming. You are released, free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That concludes our proceedings today. We shall -- is there any matter you want to raise, Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Just one brief one, Your Honour, consistent with the Trial Chamber's orders. At the conclusion of the evidence, we would like to retrieve the copies of the notes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The Defence, of course, should give those back, as ordered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And if the accused has any copies. Any copies that they've made other than the two we gave them, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll endeavour. We're going to have to take some time to do that, but we will comply, obviously, with the order and produce that. That are some notes written on it, on the actual copies. If we can merely have it destroyed with our presence as well, if that would be okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're happy if they give them to Mr. Bos and he can shred them. It's just that they're returned and destroyed, is all we're concerned about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, hand them back to the registrar, and there should be no difficulty about them. As far as the future scheduling of the case is concerned, the next hearing will be on the 21st of September. There will be a hearing for three weeks. We have now completed our plans for the autumn. We have borne in mind everything that's said about this case and, of course, the importance of finishing it. However, we have to try another matter and so we have to fit both in, and the upshot is that after the 9th of October, the next hearings will be the 23rd of November and the 11th of December. And if I could add this for the Prosecution, that, of course, it's not possible always to time these things accurately, but in line with your earlier estimates, we would hope that the Prosecution case is concluded by that date in December, the Prosecution would have that in mind. Then we will adjourn until the 21st of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 1.06 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 21st day of September, 1998, at 9.00 a.m.
